extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic and the scientific method (philosophers, naturalists, scientists learning classification and error analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for constructing natural classifications and arranging classes into series to facilitate inductive inquiries; plus a systematic taxonomy of fallacies (apparent evidence that is not real evidence) and guidance for detecting and avoiding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by important common properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Classification ... is to make us think of those objects together which have the greatest number of important common properties; and which, therefore, we have oftenest occasion ... for taking into joint consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form groups so that the ideas of objects are brought into the order most conducive to inductive inquiries generally; prioritize the most important characters when forming natural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for classification serving a particular inductive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The requisites of a classification intended to facilitate the study of a particular phenomenon, are, first to bring into one class all Kinds of things which exhibit that phenomenon ... and, secondly, to arrange those Kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most of it, and terminating with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the purpose is a specific inquiry, choose the phenomenon as the groundwork of classification; include all instances showing the phenomenon and order them by degree of manifestation to reveal laws via concomitant variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use series to enable Concomitant Variations method
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the instances ... into the order which is implied in one of the four Methods of Experimental Inquiry ... the fourth Method, that of Concomitant Variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange objects so that increasing/decreasing together (or co-disappearing) facts can be observed, since such concomitant variation suggests cause-effect or common-cause relations; series are instrumental where artificial experiments are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a type-species to recognize identity across degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a classification of this sort ... requires the power of recognizing the essential similarity of a phenomenon, in its minuter degrees ... the assumption of a type-species is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select as type the kind exhibiting the constitutive properties in highest degree; treat other varieties as degenerations from that type so that subtle/rudimentary instances can be recognized and compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions must reflect variation in main phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary divisions must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately, but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When breaking a series into classes (Orders, Families, Genera), cut at points where marked changes in intensity of the principal phenomenon coincide with conspicuous changes in miscellaneous properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural affinity as main principle of division
rubrics_metrics.description: The main principle of division must of course be natural affinity; the classes formed must be natural groups; and the formation of these has already been sufficiently treated of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups should be constituted by the most important characters (natural affinities) so that classifications are scientifically defensible and not arbitrary collections of traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal distribution should preserve series ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Each family should, if possible, be so subdivided, that one portion of it shall stand higher and the other lower, though of course contiguous, in the general scale; and only when this is impossible is it allowable to ground the remaining subdivisions on characters having no determinable connection with the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within groups, attempt to order subgroups by their position in the overall series; avoid subdivisions based on unrelated characters unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: When special-purpose classification becomes general
rubrics_metrics.description: There are cases in which the arrangement required for the special purpose becomes the determining principle of the classification of the same objects for general purposes ... when those laws ... enact so principal a part in the general character and history of those objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the phenomenon of special inquiry predominates in determining most properties of objects, the special classification can legitimately serve as the general one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits: series not always applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case even of vegetables, the natural arrangement has not been carried beyond the formation of natural groups. Naturalists have found ... it impossible to form those groups into any series, the terms of which correspond to real gradations in the phenomenon of vegetative or organic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the main phenomenon exhibits measurable gradations across the set; where differences in degree are not marked, classification-by-series is impracticable and ordinary natural groupings suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply principles of natural arrangement beyond biology
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the scientific arrangements of organic nature afford as yet the only complete example ... those principles are applicable to all cases in which mankind are called upon to bring the various parts of any extensive subject into mental co-ordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same scientific conditions when arranging matters of art, business, or law (e.g., code organization); studying biological classification is good preparatory discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat fallacies as catalog of apparent but not real evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of the varieties of apparent evidence which are not real evidence, is an enumeration of Fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically enumerate varieties of apparent evidence that can mislead; analysis of fallacies is essential to a complete philosophy of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish moral and intellectual causes of error
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of erroneous opinions are twofold, moral and intellectual. Of these, the moral do not fall within the compass of this work ... But the moral causes ... do not act directly, but by means of the intellectual causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing error, focus on intellectual causes (how evidence is processed), while recognizing moral causes (indifference, bias) primarily act by distorting intellectual operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori / natural prejudices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Simple Inspection, or Fallacies a priori ... all cases in which a proposition is believed and held for true, literally without any extrinsic evidence ... or those ... in which simple inspection creates a presumption in favor of a proposition ... sufficient to cause the strict principles of a regular induction to be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for beliefs accepted on presumption or apparent self-evidence; these natural prejudices often bypass proper induction and should be interrogated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Inference vs Fallacies of Simple Inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: This gives rise to the first great distinction, that between Fallacies of Inference and Fallacies of Simple Inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify fallacies by whether the supposed connection is inferred from evidence or admitted on inspection; different detection and remedy strategies apply to each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion (vagueness, ambiguity, shifting premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: This gives existence to a class of fallacies ... Fallacies of Confusion; comprehending, among others, all those which have their source in language, whether arising from the vagueness or ambiguity of our terms, or from casual associations with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to equivocation, vague terms, and unconscious substitution of premises or conclusions during reasoning; make concepts precise to avoid these errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-principle for classifying fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: We may arrange them, at our choice, on either of two principles; according to the cause which makes them appear to be evidence, not being so; or according to the particular kind of evidence which they simulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building a taxonomy of fallacies, use both the causal origin and the form of seeming evidence they imitate to organize and detect them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Induction: Observation vs Generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Induction, where the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous, may be termed Fallacies of Observation ... The other class of inductive fallacies, in which the facts are correct, but the conclusion not warranted by them, are properly denominated Fallacies of Generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate inductive errors that stem from faulty/missed/incorrect observation from those that overgeneralize from correct observations; remediation differs (better observation vs restraining generalization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Deduction and Fallacies of Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: There remain ... those in which the premises of the ratiocination do not bear out its conclusion; the various cases, in short, of vicious argumentation, provided against by the rules of the syllogism. We shall call these, Fallacies of Ratiocination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deductive contexts check whether premises (however obtained) logically support the conclusion; apply syllogistic rules to detect vicious reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors may mix classes and often hide in suppressed premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous arguments do not admit of such a sharply cut division ... In all arguments ... some of the links are suppressed ... and it is in those steps ... that the error oftenest lurks. In order to detect the fallacy, the proposition thus silently assumed must be supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing an argument, make implicit premises explicit; reconstruct full argumentation to reveal hidden assumptions or shifts that produce the fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-fold source of apparent evidentiary relation: observed conjunction or prior association
rubrics_metrics.description: The supposed connection ... may either be a conclusion from evidence ... or may be admitted without any such ground; admitted ... on its own evidence; embraced as self-evident ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a perceived evidentiary link arises from observed frequency/conjunction or from mental habits/associations; treatment differs (seek empirical test vs examine habitual presumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguard against fallacies: habit of reasoning well
rubrics_metrics.description: The only complete safeguard against reasoning ill, is the habit of reasoning well; familiarity with the principles of correct reasoning, and practice in applying those principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate continual practice in correct methods of induction and ratiocination; training and vigilance reduce susceptibility to fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of presumption that A evidences B (error rooted in assumed conjunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: We can not regard one fact as evidentiary of another, unless we believe that the two are always, or in the majority of cases, conjoined ... When we infer some fact from some other fact which does not really prove it, we either have admitted, or ... ought to admit, some groundless general proposition respecting the conjunction of the two phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ask what general proposition is being tacitly assumed when treating one fact as evidence of another; test whether the asserted conjunction is real or groundless.
